That's a good question, it's been a few years since I started the project 😅
I originally got started because I wanted to learn how to use IDA and thought it should be possible to make my Wii U Pro controllers work with the system

I'd spent a couple of years prior lurking on the reswitched discord keeping up with the state of switch hacking, so I had some idea of the tools/scripts etc that people had made available to simplify dumping and decrypting firmware files, loading them into IDA and matching symbols etc
From there it was looking at existing documentation on switchbrew, asking questions on reswitched, messing around with various modules in IDA looking for clues about the Bluetooth implementation etc
Eventually I found some strings in the bluetooth module that matched perfectly with strings found in Bluedroid, the Android bluetooth stack
So from then I was lucky enough to be able to refer to the Android source code to get an idea of function arguments, event structures etc

I was able to use this info to infer/guess some of the bluetooth IPC arguments, and event structures exposed by the bluetooth module. The next step was to implement some of the IPC calls in libnx using this knowledge and see if I could write a homebrew that could interact with bluetooth in some way

I also made use of a tool called Ilia, which is capable of logging IPC on specified interfaces and comes with a dissector to open the captures in wireshark for inspection. I made a bunch of captures while connecting and using my Switch Pro Controller on the console and used this to figure out even more of the IPC arguments

The idea to MITM everything didn't actually come until much later, when I was dealing with a whole bunch of random crashes due to all the inconsistencies I was creating by calling internal functions that other things were supposed to be managing. I thought  why not try to trick the system into thinking these _are_ pro controllers and letting the parts of the system that were in charge of managing bluetooth stuff do their thing and not get in their way

The key was figuring out that i could not only use atmosphere to MITM the IPC, but also steal the event handles obtained via IPC calls and MITM events too by swapping in my own fake handles that I could signal instead when I was done altering event data

The rest has just been spending an ungodly amount of time poking around in IDA to figure out most of the logic of the bluetooth module, debugging the running service with gdb to see internal data and which functions get hit during certain operations, writing binary patches based on this knowledge to modify the behaviour of the bluetooth module, and writing a bunch of python scripts to automate some of this...
And that's about where we are today

Very unlikely. On top of this stuff being very time consuming, the reason software like Mission Control is possible on Switch is because of several key factors that work in our favour...
1) We have a bootrom exploit, that allows us to load CFW/modify processes at boot time. This allows us to modify behaviour before initialisation of the bluetooth driver occurs, and makes MITM of services possible
2) The microservices design of the OS means the OS functionality is broken down into a whole bunch of dedicated services, with an IPC mechanism for accessing each others functionality. This means there is a whole bunch of functionality that we can access directly, simply by making the appropriate IPC call, and gives plenty of surface to MITM calls between services, where we can steal handles to system events and modify other data in-flight.
3) Because of the IPC mechanisms, and symbols that people have found both in older firmwares, and factory leftovers etc, the official names of a majority of the IPC functions have been recovered. In many cases, this high level information is enough to make use of a function without having to dig into its internals. It also gives us plenty of starting points to work backwards from to aid in reverse engineering of other internal code.
4) The switch scene is very active and has many highly skilled contributors. As a result we have many great tools, and documentation of system internals.
I'm sure there are other things I haven't thought of too
